title: AI Condition Monitoring: How It Works
summary: AI condition monitoring applies machine learning to vibration, temperature, and current data to detect equipment faults early. See how it works.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- AI condition monitoring applies machine learning to vibration, temperature, current, and acoustic data from sensors on rotating equipment, so developing faults are flagged while readings still sit below fixed alarm limits.
- It works in two layers: anomaly detection spots when an asset departs from its own normal behavior, and fault classification names the likely cause, such as bearing wear, cavitation, or looseness.
- Value depends on deployment and integration as much as on the model: cellular connectivity removes plant network barriers, and CMMS integration turns each alert into a planned work order.


Most plants already practice some form of condition monitoring. A technician walks a vibration route once a month, an infrared camera comes out before a shutdown, and the control system trips a motor when its temperature crosses a limit.


AI condition monitoring keeps the same goal and changes the method. Sensors stay on the machine, data arrives continuously, and a model compares each new reading against what that specific machine looks like when it is healthy. A bearing defect that would not trip a 7.1 mm/s vibration alarm for weeks can show up as a change in pattern much earlier.


## What Is AI Condition Monitoring?


AI condition monitoring is the continuous measurement of equipment health signals combined with machine learning models that detect and diagnose developing faults. It extends traditional[asset condition monitoring](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/asset-condition-monitoring) by replacing fixed thresholds and periodic manual review with learned, asset-specific baselines and automated fault classification.


It sits within the broader field of[physical AI](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/physical-ai) : AI that reads real physical conditions through sensors rather than working only on business data. The models reason about bearings, impellers, windings, and couplings, so the physics of how machines fail shapes how the system is built.


## AI Condition Monitoring vs Traditional Threshold Monitoring


Threshold monitoring raises an alarm when one value crosses one fixed limit; AI condition monitoring compares many signal features against each asset's learned normal behavior and known fault patterns. The result is earlier detection, a likely cause attached to each alert, and fewer nuisance alarms during normal speed and load changes.


Dimension Traditional threshold monitoring AI condition monitoring


What is measured Usually one overall value per signal


Many features per signal: RMS, kurtosis, spectral peaks, envelope, trends


How limits are set Generic values from standards or OEM sheets


Baselines learned for each asset at its own speed and load


When it alerts When the value crosses the limit, often late


When patterns change, often while overall values still look normal


Alert content "High vibration" or "high temperature"


Likely failure mode, supporting evidence, and severity

Speed and load are inputs to the model


Signals combined Each signal judged separately


Vibration, current, temperature, and acoustic data correlated

Continuous or near-continuous sensor data


Expert time Spent screening alarms and walking routes

Best fit Simple, constant-speed assets with known limits


Critical rotating assets, variable duty, large fleets


Thresholds still have a role. A hard trip limit protects a machine from destroying itself, and that safety function belongs in the control system. AI condition monitoring adds the early warning that a trip limit was not designed to give.


## How AI Processes Equipment Signals


AI processes equipment signals by capturing vibration, current, temperature, and acoustic data, extracting features that describe machine condition, and then running two kinds of models: anomaly detection to find departures from normal and fault classification to identify the cause.


### The four signal types


Each signal reveals a different part of machine health.


Signal What it reveals Example faults


Vibration Mechanical forces and impacts in the rotating system


Imbalance, misalignment, looseness, bearing defects, gear wear


Current Electrical health of the motor and the load it drives


Broken rotor bars, winding imbalance, cavitation, process overload


Temperature Heat from friction, electrical loss, or poor cooling


Lubrication failure, overloaded bearings, winding insulation stress


Acoustic and ultrasonic High-frequency friction and impacts


Early lubrication problems, cavitation, leaks


[Industrial vibration analysis](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-vibration-analysis) has the longest history of the four and the deepest library of known fault signatures. Current, temperature, and acoustic data fill in faults that vibration sees poorly, such as electrical problems in the motor itself.


### Feature extraction


Raw waveforms are too large and noisy to compare directly. Feature extraction compresses them into numbers that describe condition.


Common features include RMS (overall energy), peak and crest factor (how large the biggest impacts are), kurtosis (how impulsive the signal is), FFT spectral peaks at running speed and its harmonics, and envelope spectra that isolate repeating bearing impacts. For current, features include phase imbalance and sidebands around line frequency.


Our guide to[AI fault detection](https://tractian.com/en/blog/ai-fault-detection) explains each feature in depth, including a worked calculation of bearing defect frequencies.


### Anomaly detection vs fault classification


Anomaly detection answers "is this machine behaving differently than usual?" Fault classification answers "what is wrong with it?" A useful system does both.


Anomaly detection Fault classification


Training data Normal operation of the asset


Labeled examples of known faults


Output Deviation score: how far from normal


Named fault and confidence, such as "outer race defect"


Strength Catches unexpected or rare problems


Tells the technician what to inspect and which parts to order


Weakness Says something changed, not what


Can miss faults it was not trained on


Typical use First screen on each monitored asset


Second step once an anomaly or known signature appears


In practice, the anomaly model raises a flag, the classifier checks the features against known signatures, and the alert goes out with both the deviation and the most likely cause.


### Walkthrough: an alert on a pump motor


Here is an illustrative sequence on a 4-pole induction motor driving a centrifugal cooling water pump. The timeline is hypothetical and simplified to show how the layers work together.


1. **Week 0:** Sensors on the motor and pump bearings establish a baseline across normal flow rates.
2. **Week 3:** Kurtosis on the pump outboard bearing rises from about 3 to above 5. Overall vibration barely changes. The anomaly model flags a deviation.
3. **Week 3, same day:** The classifier finds a peak in the envelope spectrum at the outer race defect frequency. The alert reads "probable outer race defect, early stage" with the spectrum attached.
4. **Week 4:** The planner confirms a replacement bearing is in stock and schedules the swap for the next planned line stop.
5. **Week 6:** The bearing is replaced during the stop. The removed bearing shows a small spall on the outer race, which confirms the diagnosis and becomes a labeled example for future training.


Without continuous monitoring, the first sign might have been noise from the pump months later, followed by an unplanned stop.


## Failure Types AI Condition Monitoring Detects


AI condition monitoring detects failure modes that change a machine's vibration, current, temperature, or acoustic signals. Six of the most common on rotating equipment are bearing wear, winding degradation, cavitation, misalignment, imbalance, and looseness.


Many machine failures trace back to one of these, which is why they are the core of most detection libraries. For general background, see our glossary entry on[equipment failure](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/equipment-failure) .


### Bearing wear


A defect on a bearing race or rolling element creates a small impact each time a rolling element passes over it. These impacts repeat at frequencies set by bearing geometry and shaft speed: BPFO for the outer race, BPFI for the inner race, BSF for the rolling elements, and FTF for the cage.


Early impacts excite high-frequency resonances long before overall vibration rises, so kurtosis and envelope analysis catch them first. Ultrasonic data and temperature help confirm whether the root cause is lubrication.


### Winding degradation


Motor stator insulation weakens with heat, moisture, contamination, and voltage spikes. A short between turns creates a hot spot and unbalances the magnetic field.


Current data shows this as imbalance between phases. Temperature rises, and vibration at twice line frequency can increase. Early detection allows a planned rewind instead of an in-service failure.


### Cavitation


Cavitation occurs when pump inlet pressure falls below the liquid's vapor pressure, so vapor bubbles form and then collapse against the impeller. The collapses produce broadband high-frequency vibration and noise and erode the impeller over time.


AI recognizes it from a raised high-frequency noise floor, fluctuating motor current, and correlation with process conditions such as low tank level or a throttled suction valve.


### Misalignment


Misalignment happens when coupled shafts do not share a centerline. Angular misalignment tends to show as high axial vibration at 1x running speed. Parallel misalignment tends to show as high radial vibration at 2x.


Left in place, misalignment overloads bearings and seals, so catching it early prevents a second failure later.


### Imbalance


Imbalance means the rotor's mass is not evenly distributed around its axis. It produces a strong radial peak at 1x running speed with a stable phase.


The force rises with the square of speed, so a fan that is acceptable at half speed can be severe at full speed. Buildup on blades and erosion are common causes.


### Looseness


Looseness comes in two main forms. Structural looseness, such as a cracked base or loose hold-down bolts, often shows at 1x with a strong directional difference between horizontal and vertical readings.


Rotating looseness, such as a bearing loose on its shaft or in its housing, produces many harmonics of running speed and sometimes half-order peaks (0.5x, 1.5x). The waveform can look clipped. Because looseness amplifies other faults, it often shows up alongside imbalance or misalignment.

## Edge vs Cloud Deployment


Edge deployment runs analysis on the sensor or a local gateway; cloud deployment sends data to remote servers. Most AI condition monitoring systems use a hybrid: the edge computes features and screens for urgent events, and the cloud trains models and compares assets across a fleet.


### Latency tradeoffs


Most mechanical faults develop over days to months, so a few seconds of delay rarely matters for detection. Latency matters for fast events, such as a sudden vibration spike on high-speed equipment, where local processing can raise an alert without a network round trip.


The bigger constraint is usually bandwidth. High-resolution vibration captures are large, and sending them raw from hundreds of sensors is expensive or impossible on a weak connection. Extracting features at the edge reduces the data to what the model needs.


### Hybrid architecture


Layer What runs there Why


Sensor Sampling, basic features, fast event detection


Reduces data volume and catches urgent changes locally


Gateway Aggregation, buffering during outages, transmission


Keeps data safe when connectivity drops


Cloud Model training, fleet comparison, dashboards, integrations


Large compute and data from many assets and sites


### Cellular connectivity


Many plants restrict new devices on their operational network, and getting IT approval for a firewall change can take months. Cellular-connected gateways sidestep that by sending data over a mobile network instead of the plant LAN, so no plant network access is required.


This also helps in remote or spread-out sites, such as pump stations or mining operations, where wired networks do not reach each asset. Tractian uses this design: the sensor captures data on the asset, a gateway relays it over 4G/LTE, and the AI analysis runs in Tractian's cloud.


For a deeper technical view, see our guide to[edge AI for industrial plants](https://tractian.com/en/blog/edge-ai-industrial-plants) .


## Integration: CMMS, ERP, SCADA


AI condition monitoring plugs into existing workflows by sending diagnosed alerts to the CMMS as work orders, linking parts and costs to the ERP, and reading process context from SCADA or historians. Integration is what turns a detected fault into a scheduled repair.


### CMMS


The CMMS is where maintenance work gets planned and recorded. A good integration creates a work order from an alert, attaches the diagnosis and evidence, and sets priority based on asset criticality and fault severity.


The loop runs both ways. When the technician closes the work order and records what they found, that confirmation helps validate and improve the model.


### ERP


ERP integration connects the alert to parts, purchasing, and cost. If a bearing replacement is predicted, the planner can check stock and raise a purchase request early, instead of paying for expedited shipping after a failure.


### SCADA and historians


SCADA systems and historians hold process data: flow, pressure, speed, and run status. Feeding this context into the model helps separate a real fault from a normal change in operation. A vibration rise during a speed increase is expected; the same rise at constant speed is not.


This connects condition monitoring with[industrial automation](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/industrial-automation) systems without replacing them. The control system keeps controlling the process, and the monitoring system watches the health of the equipment that runs it.


### Integration checklist


Use these questions when assessing how a platform will fit your workflow:


1. Which CMMS platforms does it integrate with natively, and which need custom work?
2. Does it create work orders automatically, or only send notifications?
3. Does closed work order data flow back to the monitoring platform?
4. Is there a documented API for systems without a native connector?
5. Can it read process context from your SCADA or historian?
6. Who maintains the integration when either system updates?


For a full evaluation framework, see[how to choose an AI condition monitoring provider](https://tractian.com/en/blog/how-to-choose-ai-condition-monitoring-provider) .

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is an AI condition monitoring system?


An AI condition monitoring system is a set of sensors, connectivity, and software that continuously measures equipment health and uses machine learning to detect and diagnose developing faults. Sensors capture vibration, temperature, current, or acoustic data, models compare it to each asset's normal behavior and known fault signatures, and alerts go to maintenance teams with the likely cause attached.


### What industrial AI software can detect machine failures?


Industrial AI software that detects machine failures combines sensor data with models trained to recognize failure signatures. Look for software that identifies specific failure modes, such as bearing defects, imbalance, misalignment, cavitation, and winding faults, rather than only flagging anomalies. Tractian's Smart Trac Ultra sensor combines vibration, ultrasound, temperature, and magnetic field data, and the platform adds electrical signals to detect these failure modes before failure.


### Can industrial AI predict equipment failure using vibration data?


Yes. Vibration is one of the strongest predictors of mechanical failure in rotating equipment, because faults such as bearing defects, imbalance, and misalignment produce distinct frequency patterns. AI models extract features such as RMS, kurtosis, and spectral peaks and track how they change, which can give weeks of warning for faults that develop gradually.


### Who offers scalable AI condition monitoring solutions for large fleets?


Several vendors sell AI condition monitoring for multi-site fleets, Tractian among them. Scalability depends on wireless sensors that install without major wiring, connectivity that does not depend on each plant's network, centralized dashboards across sites, and models that learn from similar assets fleet-wide. Ask vendors for references at a comparable number of assets and sites.


### Who offers turnkey AI condition monitoring packages including installation and training?


Turnkey packages bundle sensors, installation, software, and team training under one contract. When comparing offers, confirm who mounts the sensors, who sets up asset hierarchies and integrations, what training is included for technicians and planners, and what support continues after go-live. Tractian's offering includes installation and training by certified specialists, and Tractian's standard deployment gets customers fully operational within 14 days.


### Who supplies retrofit AI condition monitoring kits for legacy equipment?


Retrofit kits add wireless sensors to existing motors, pumps, fans, and compressors without changing the machine or its controls. Most AI condition monitoring vendors, including Tractian, design their sensors to mount on legacy equipment. Check mounting options, battery life, temperature and hazardous-area ratings, and whether the kit needs plant network access.


### Which AI condition monitoring providers offer SLA-backed accuracy guarantees?


SLA terms vary widely, and few providers publish them openly, so ask for the SLA document during evaluation. Check what is actually covered: platform uptime, alert response time, analyst review time, or detection performance. Be cautious with accuracy claims that do not define how a missed fault or false alarm is counted.


### Can AI condition monitoring manage multi-site fleets?


Yes, when the platform centralizes data from many plants in one view, uses consistent asset hierarchies, and lets teams compare similar machines across sites. Fleet data also improves models, because a failure pattern seen on one pump can help detect it earlier on similar pumps elsewhere. Connectivity that works independently of each site's network makes rollout faster.


### What are the best entry-level AI condition monitoring platforms for small-to-medium businesses?


For smaller plants, the best fit is usually a platform with wireless sensors that install in minutes, a subscription that scales by asset count, and alerts that include the diagnosis so no in-house vibration analyst is needed. Start with five to twenty critical assets and expand once the first catches are confirmed. Our AI condition monitoring software buyer's guide compares options on these points.


### Do AI condition monitoring platforms have an open API?


Many do, but the scope varies. Check whether the API exposes raw readings, features, alerts, and asset data, whether it supports both reading and writing, and whether documentation is public. An API matters most when you need to feed alerts into a system without a native connector or pull data into your own analytics.


### How does AI condition monitoring integrate with a CMMS?


The usual pattern is that an alert creates or suggests a work order in the CMMS, with the diagnosis, evidence, and priority attached. When the technician closes the order, the findings flow back to confirm the diagnosis. Native connectors are faster to set up than custom API work, so check which CMMS platforms a vendor supports out of the box.


### What is the payback period for AI condition monitoring?


Payback depends on how many failures the monitored assets have, what each costs, and the program cost. Plants that start with critical assets that fail often tend to see faster payback, because a single avoided failure can cover a large share of annual cost. Build your estimate from your own failure history using the ROI framework in our AI condition monitoring cost guide. For a benchmark, the Verdantix study commissioned by Tractian modeled an 8-month break-even point for a modeled multi-site manufacturer.


### How long does AI condition monitoring deployment take?


Wireless sensor installation can take minutes per asset, so physical installation for a pilot of a few dozen machines is often a matter of days. Models then need a baseline period of normal operation, typically days to a few weeks, before anomaly detection is fully tuned. CMMS integration and team training run in parallel and depend on your systems and internal approvals.
